title: Switch — core service health
description: What switch-core reports about itself. Metric definitions live in core/switch_core/observability/catalogue.py; this dashboard is checked into deploy/observability/ in the switch repository, so edit it there rather than here.

definition.content:
**Releases.** Every panel on this dashboard can be narrowed to one release of switch-core.

1. Pick a release in **version** at the top of the page. Every panel below follows it; `*` means all releases.
2. Pick what to compare it with in **baseline**. Only the comparison panels in this section use it.
3. Set the time range (top right) wide enough to cover both releases. Releases replace each other, so they are usually live at different times: the comparison panels show the release line and the baseline line side by side along the time axis, not on top of each other.

A release is the version in `core/pyproject.toml`. A build between releases reports the last release it followed. In the scorecard a failure column reads 0 when that release recorded none. An empty p95 column means percentiles are not enabled for `version` on that metric (see the README).

**Prod or dev:** open **Saved views** at the left of the variable bar and pick **Prod** (service `switch-core`) or **Dev** (service `switch-core-dev`). Version 0.27.0 is hidden: it came from instances that no longer run.

definition.content: **Release events.** Counted from the usage events switch-core sends when usage reporting is on (`TELEMETRY_ENABLED`), so a deployment that exports no metrics still shows here. They follow the same **version**, **baseline** and **service** pickers as the panels above, and reach back only as far as the log index keeps events. Installs are distinct deployments. The same service name can cover more than one, for example a production server and every self-hosted server left at the default name.

definition.content: **Is it working?** Each dependency reports 1 when its last check passed and 0 when it failed. Only the database takes a pod out of service. With one replica that empties the service; with several, traffic moves to the pods that still pass. A crashed bridge is a real fault that is deliberately not fatal.

Agents connected
Bridges running
Consumers running (read loops)
Event-loop lag (ms, worst)

definition.content: **HTTP.** Routes are templates, never resolved paths — a path carries an id per request and would be a new series each time. Anything the router could not place is folded into `unmatched`.

definition.title: Requests per second, by outcome (none = no response sent)

definition.content:
**Rooms.** Delivery lag is the age of a message when it reached a recipient, measured per delivery. Delivery failures are the exceptions the delivery loop swallows on purpose so one bad room cannot stop the others — which is also what makes them invisible without this.

**Sent and delivered are not the same unit.** A send is one write; a delivery is one recipient, so a room with five clients delivers five times per send. Delivered sitting above sent is normal. What matters is the shape of each line, not the gap between them.

definition.title: Messages per second: sent (writes) vs delivered (per recipient)
Delivery, routing and message-observer failures, and rows too old to replay, per second
Delivery lag p95 / p99 (ms) — needs distribution mapping, see README

definition.content: **Bridges.** Inbound is counted where every platform event already funnels through; outbound at the relay, so a human actor's own echo and a room with no channel are not counted as traffic nobody sent.

definition.title: Bridge events in per second, by bridge and platform
Bridge events out per second, by bridge and platform
Bridge errors per second, by bridge, platform and direction

definition.content:
**Resources.** Reported by the process about itself — there is no infrastructure agent in this cluster. Event-loop lag is the one no agent could produce: the server is single-threaded, so one blocking call stalls every room and bridge at once, and from outside that looks like an unrelated timeout somewhere else.

Pool overflow is zero until the pool is full, then counts the connections opened beyond it — saturation shows as in-use approaching size.

definition.content: **Things that are lost.** Each of these is a message or an event that existed and did not arrive. They are counted rather than only logged because every one of them is invisible from the outside: a send that never persisted looks like a quiet room, and an agent told it missed events has no way to tell anyone else.

definition.content: **Shared room reads.** Each fill is one database read standing in for one per member of the room, so fills against deliveries is the saving. A fallback (behind, evicted, unwatched, gave_up) is a transport reading the database itself: it costs a read, never a message.

definition.content:
**Decision routing.** With auto-route on, a person's untagged message waits while a decision backend picks which agent, if any, should answer it. Decisions and failures count requests to a backend; settled counts messages, however each one ended, and wait is how long the person waited for that. `backend` is the kind of backend asked, never which endpoint or workspace.

**`model` is the model that answered** (`gemini-decision-1`, `strands-decider-E4B`, `claude-haiku-5-5`, ...), so a change of model behind the server default shows as one line ending and another starting. `unknown` is a decision with no answer (a timeout, an error), `workspace_endpoint` a workspace's own endpoint, whose model name is never kept, and `other` a name that isn't plain. On nonprod a decision delivers at a confidence of 0.80 or more.

**Waiting messages are server-wide.** Every pod reports the same pending count and oldest age, so they are read with max; a sum would multiply them by the number of pods. The health check exists only when the server has a default decision endpoint.

definition.content: **Hosted agents (cloud machines).** Read from the machines' status reports and the hosted controller service's calls: no ids, only counts and fixed words. Gauges come from one Core process (the hosted metrics lock holder) and leave out reports older than 3 minutes. A machine gone silent shows as reporting below expected; a machine stopped by its owner or for idleness isn't expected. `backend` is the kind of machine: `vm` for a v1 machine, `box` for a hosted agents v2 box. The box panels at the end fill only with hosted agents v2 on. Filter by `$service`, and by `$flint_env` for the deployment's environment.

definition.content: **Hosted agents v2 (boxes).** Empty unless `HOSTED_BOX_PROVISIONING` is on. What only a box reports, beside the v1 panels above, which cover boxes too under `backend:box`: the operator's open alerts, sessions waiting for room, restarts, out-of-memory kills and evictions, the memory guard and valve, the provider gateway, and box memory. Counts and fixed words only.
